businessScenario.customerSituation: New product line with shared risk

module_LifeCycle.headline: Business Servitization live cycle - Pro and Cons – Rational arguments

lifeCycleStage.name: Machine Purchase Investment
lifeCycleStage.description: Consider what the pro’s and con’s of owning a machine including investment, budgets, CAPEX/OPEX versus use only are.

proArgument.note: More time to focus on product
proArgument.explanation: The new direction would let shopfloor staff focus on the product and the customer's core business instead of the surrounding effort required to produce it.

contraArgument.explanation: The change could cause the company to lose talent, either voluntarily or involuntarily, which would be harmful to the business.

proArgument.explanation: The customer would not need to make an upfront investment in the equipment.

contraArgument.explanation: Avoiding the upfront investment would most likely result in a higher total cost of ownership over time.

proArgument.explanation: The service OPEX agreement would provide the service provider with continuous positive revenue.

contraArgument.explanation: The service provider must make an initial upfront investment before receiving returns over time.

lifeCycleStage.name: Installation & Commissioning
lifeCycleStage.description: Consider how the installation and commissioning process is influenced when buying versus using a machine you don’t own.

proArgument.explanation: The shopfloor can focus on chocolate-industry best practices and ensure that the equipment is installed according to established guidelines and the company's experience.

contraArgument.explanation: Miscommunication and misunderstandings could create risks and trust issues when the technological and chocolate-production perspectives are brought together.

proArgument.explanation: The installation would be delivered as a turnkey solution, leaving the customer with nothing to do before the machine is up and running.
Installing its own equipment would give the service provider more control over installation and commissioning.

contraArgument.explanation: Because the installation takes place at the customer's premises, it requires more coordination and therefore creates greater complexity.

lifeCycleStage.name: Standard Operation
lifeCycleStage.description: Consider how your workforce and standard operation processes are influenced by the fact that your company or the manufacturer is owing the asset.

proArgument.explanation: The same number of people could operate more machines in parallel, increasing operational capacity and potentially improving production.

contraArgument.explanation: Over time, shopfloor staff could lose the ability to operate the machines themselves and become heavily reliant on the service partner.

proArgument.explanation: The customer would know exactly how much it must pay each month, with no unexpected costs.
Operating the equipment under the service model would continue to generate recurring revenue for the service provider.

contraArgument.explanation: Standard operation under the service model would bring increased complexity for the service provider.

lifeCycleStage.name: Maintenance And Repair
lifeCycleStage.description: Consider how the maintenance process is influenced by the ownership of the asset and how your maintenance planning and operation will be done.

proArgument.explanation: Predictive maintenance would remove the need for the customer to create its own maintenance plan; IPCO would notify it when components such as bearings need to be changed.

contraArgument.explanation: The customer would be locked into the vendor's ecosystem and unable to obtain maintenance services elsewhere.

proArgument.explanation: The customer would reduce personnel costs because it would no longer need to maintain the same maintenance capability in-house.

contraArgument.explanation: Maintenance would be less flexible: the customer could not simply schedule it during a period of lower production and might have to wait for the next available service slot.

proArgument.explanation: With full control, the service provider could perform maintenance when it is actually needed instead of following a fixed schedule.

contraArgument.explanation: The increased complexity would remain a negative factor for the service provider during maintenance and repair.

lifeCycleStage.name: Breakdown Management
lifeCycleStage.description: Consider there is a serious breakdown how will flexibility and agility be influence by you or an external company managing the breakdown and getting the machine up and running again.

proArgument.explanation: A service-level agreement would define how quickly a breakdown is expected to be resolved.

contraArgument.explanation: Even with a defined resolution time, the customer would still incur a loss for every hour of downtime.

proArgument.explanation: The service arrangement would share breakdown-related risks between the parties.

contraArgument.note: You get what you pay for
contraArgument.explanation: A lower-priced agreement would provide a lower service level, potentially including longer reaction times, so the customer must pay enough for the service it requires.

proArgument.explanation: Breakdowns should not occur if the equipment is operated in the way the service provider specifies.

contraArgument.explanation: The service provider would nevertheless carry a financial risk if a breakdown occurs.

lifeCycleStage.name: Decommissioning & End of Life Treatment
lifeCycleStage.description: Consider your company wants to get rid of their old machine what costs, responsibilities and efforts will be involved for decommissioning the old machine.

proArgument.explanation: The customer would not have to perform the decommissioning or deal with the resulting waste.

contraArgument.explanation: Although the customer would not need to handle decommissioning or waste, the process would still cost time.

proArgument.explanation: The customer would not incur costs for scrapping the equipment.

contraArgument.explanation: Once the equipment is decommissioned, it would be removed and the customer could no longer use it beyond its planned lifespan, even if it had effectively been paid for.

proArgument.explanation: At the end of its life, the equipment could retain residual value that belongs to the service provider.

contraArgument.explanation: The service provider would incur costs to handle the equipment at end of life and might also need to refinance it.

container_DifferentScenariosRated.headline: What are the compelling reasons for IPCO Customers to say this level is perfect for our business scenario!

explanation.explanation: Only a small increase in sales was expected at Level 2, so the impact on turnover was rated +1.
Profit could increase through value-added services, such as fast-track support when a customer urgently needs a replacement, which supported the +3 rating.
The team could not identify any impact on cash flow at Level 2, so it assigned a rating of 0.
The team could not identify any impact on the credit rating at Level 2, so it assigned a rating of 0.
Level 2 provides somewhat more predictability for production planning, but not a large improvement, which led to the +1 rating.
Equipment degradation could be detected somewhat earlier, but the service would still be reactive rather than predictive, supporting the +2 rating.
The service could reveal indicators of quality degradation, but it would still react after signs appear rather than predict them, which supported the +2 rating.
Downtime was expected to improve to a similar moderate extent as the other operational measures, while the service would remain reactive, resulting in a +2 rating.
Equipment health data could reduce crises and improve satisfaction, although some employees might resist changing established ways of working; this mixed effect supported the +2 rating.
Employees might need less direct interaction with machines when fixing problems, providing a small safety benefit and supporting the +1 rating.
More information from the machine would help employees learn more about it and improve their skills, which supported the +3 rating.

From IPCO's perspective, smart equipment creates a stronger negative impact because the customer owns the data and can share it with competitors; from the customer's perspective, the impact is smaller because the data remains at its premises.
No security impact was identified for IPCO because the data remains on the customer side, while the customer received a negative rating because IPCO would gain access to its data.
The team could not identify any liability impact for either party at Level 2, so both perspectives were rated 0.
Level 2 could create somewhat more trust, but the relationship would not yet involve shared risk, which led to the +1 partnership rating.
The Level 3 service offering was expected to provide a stronger sales argument and enable IPCO to sell more, supporting the +3 turnover rating.
The additional sales expected from the Level 3 offering should bring in more money, which supported the +3 profit rating.
Selling more was expected to have a positive effect on cash flow, supporting the +2 rating.
The team expected that higher sales could improve the credit rating, although it expressed this cautiously, resulting in a +1 rating.
More influence, more data, and the ability to adjust operations over time were expected to improve the customer's production planning substantially, supporting the +4 rating.
Having more information would allow the parties to improve equipment effectiveness, which supported the +4 rating.
The team did not expect product quality to increase substantially at Level 3, so it assigned only a +1 rating.
Better knowledge of the machines and their processes was expected to reduce production downtime from the customer's perspective, supporting the +3 rating.
Employees were expected to perform more qualified and interesting work and potentially move higher in the hierarchy, which supported the +3 satisfaction rating.
No direct safety impact was identified, so the team assigned only a slight positive rating of +1.
Level 3 would involve higher-quality work and therefore greater employee skill requirements, supporting the +3 rating.
From the customer's perspective, Level 3 creates a risk that its intellectual property could leak, which led to the -2 rating.
The increased connectivity at Level 3 introduces security risks for the customer, which supported the -3 rating.
IPCO would carry greater liability because the increased connectivity creates a risk that customer data could be lost, which led to the -2 rating.
The team regarded partnership as the most important aspect of Level 3, which supported the maximum positive rating of +5.
The team expected Level 4 to increase turnover quite dramatically, which supported the +3 rating.
Profit would rise less than turnover because IPCO must account for the investment and return needed to reach Level 4, which led to the +2 rating.
Level 4 would generate periodic incoming payments, creating a strongly positive cash-flow effect and supporting the +4 rating.
The credit rating could decline because Level 4 is a riskier scenario in which IPCO stands behind all the work delivered to customers, resulting in the -1 rating.
From the customer's perspective, production planning at Level 4 was expected to be almost perfect, which supported the +4 rating.
Equipment efficiency was expected to improve; the team considered ratings of +2 and +3 and assigned +3.
Value engineering at Level 4 could make the customer's end product slightly worse than before, although still within acceptable limits, which led to the -1 rating.
Employee satisfaction could suffer because people would become more replaceable in the organization, making the change difficult from the employee perspective and supporting the -2 rating.
Safety would improve because more employees could remain behind the safety line instead of approaching the machine, which supported the +3 rating.
Level 4 would reduce the skills required from employees and make hiring easier, which was treated as a positive impact and rated +3.

At Level 4, established practices for protecting intellectual property would need to evolve, creating a risk that information could be stolen and pursued through legal action; this supported the -1 rating.
Sharing data at Level 4 creates an ongoing risk of data loss, which led to the -2 security rating.
A contract would clearly specify who is liable, providing an identifiable responsible party and supporting the +2 rating.
The partnership at Level 4 was expected to be exceptionally strong, which supported the +4 rating.

container_ScenarioSummary.headline: This is what we believe is the best?

container_ValueEffortMatrix.headline: These are our joint business opportunities and Win-Win!

idea.explanation: Learning from the customer's process data could support improvements over time. The group saw greater immediate value for the customer than for IPCO when the learning is limited to one customer.
Predictable costs would benefit the customer, while regular income would benefit IPCO, making this a win for both parties.

idea.note: Customer allows access to the machine data, we share analytics & insights
idea.explanation: As a first step toward an equipment-as-a-service offering, the customer could allow IPCO to access machine data and receive relevant analytics and insights in return. This gives the customer a reason to share data and lets both parties start learning before predictive models are developed; the group noted that obtaining data from chocolate customers could be difficult.

IPCO and the customer could learn from each other's expertise: IPCO would learn more about chocolate production, while the customer would learn more about the machine and retain its own operational knowledge. The group regarded this exchange as a win for both.

The machine could become more like a utility: the customer provides the right parameters and the machine runs, making chocolate production more standardized. The group saw both benefits and drawbacks for the customer and placed its value near the middle of the matrix.
A closer partnership could mean IPCO is not immediately replaced after a mishap. The group considered that valuable for IPCO and hoped it would also be valuable for the customer.

As IPCO learns more about the customer's production and market, it could apply that knowledge to other chocolate manufacturers. The group saw an early commercial opportunity but also a possibility that the customer would face more competition later.

idea.note: Multi-site & focused learning from data => IPCO can reduce cost of operation & share at benefits
idea.explanation: Learning from data across several customers or sites could give IPCO more insight than learning from one customer's process alone. The group also discussed extending an initial data-sharing arrangement across a customer's multiple sites as the partnership develops.

module_freeAssociation.headline: What will our customers say?
module_freeAssociation.question: Think of your most important customer were business servitization would work. What will they say if IPCO approaches them with this new business model?

freeAssociation.explanation: Cadbury was identified as the English customer considered for this exercise.
The customer is expected to raise legal and compliance concerns about sharing data.

freeAssociation.note: Concerns. Risk assessment. How will be shared?
freeAssociation.explanation: The customer would want its concerns and risks assessed and a precise explanation of how the data will be shared.

freeAssociation.note: What is our profit in it?
freeAssociation.explanation: The customer would ask what financial benefit or profit it gains from the arrangement.
ICAM was identified as a new customer in the chocolate industry.

freeAssociation.note: It would raise questions related to legal aspects
freeAssociation.explanation: The proposed business model would raise questions about its legal implications.
The customer would need the arrangement to comply with its internal company policies.
The customer would ask for a clear account of the costs.

freeAssociation.note: Do you have any other customers doing this
freeAssociation.explanation: The customer would ask for references showing where IPCO has already implemented this model.
The customer would require assurance that IPCO can secure the shared data, treating this as a security, compliance, and legal concern.

freeAssociation.note: Do you have any IT security certification
freeAssociation.explanation: The customer would ask whether IPCO has IT security certifications that demonstrate compliance.
The customer would question whether IPCO can reliably provide the service; references to previous implementations would help demonstrate this capability.
The arrangement must offer a clear benefit and a clear win for the customer.

freeAssociation.note: In case of disputes, how do we prove that terms of use were followed?
freeAssociation.explanation: Documentation and logging would be needed to prove whether the agreed terms of use were followed if a dispute arises.

freeAssociation.note: How would I know that our IP (recipe) will not be revealed?
freeAssociation.explanation: IPCO and the customer must distinguish the information IPCO needs from the customer's essential confidential information and find a workable overlap that protects the recipe.
The customer would require a clear statement of what the service costs.
The customer would compare the burdens and risks of the model with the value it receives.
The question is whether the customer's R&D is focused on pure research or, as suggested in the discussion, on value engineering when finding new markets.
The customer's willingness to be a pioneer depends on its appetite for a high-risk, high-reward proposition.
Being an early participant was characterized as carrying high risk but offering the possibility of a high return.

freeAssociation.note: We own our data and recipe; we do not want to share
freeAssociation.explanation: The customer regards its data and recipe as proprietary and is therefore reluctant to share them.

freeAssociation.note: Why should I share, how does it make my life better?
freeAssociation.explanation: The customer would need a convincing explanation of how sharing data makes its work or business better.

freeAssociation.note: What you learn you can use to improve operations for other customers
freeAssociation.explanation: IPCO could apply lessons from this interaction to improve operations for other customers, while lessons learned from those customers could also benefit this customer.

freeAssociation.note: We are the chocolate experts, not you.
freeAssociation.explanation: The customer has the chocolate expertise, while IPCO knows the machines; the cooperation must find the point where IPCO can help without claiming to be a chocolate expert.
The customer is expected to regard sharing data as a significant concern.
The arrangement must clarify how risk and reward will be shared between IPCO and the customer.

freeAssociation.note: IT will be more expensive 4 us over time.
freeAssociation.explanation: If the model makes IT more expensive over time, IPCO needs a persuasive financial case showing that benefits such as less downtime, more output, or an output commitment make the additional cost worthwhile.

freeAssociation.note: Who will assume response if there is a long stop?
freeAssociation.explanation: The parties must clarify who assumes responsibility if the machine is stopped for a long time.

freeAssociation.note: What if the (end) product doesn't sell?
freeAssociation.explanation: The parties must define how far IPCO's responsibility extends, because taking over the customer's risk that the end product will not sell was considered too far-reaching.

freeAssociation.note: How can I benefit from it?
freeAssociation.explanation: The customer would look for concrete benefits in areas such as cost, reaction time, and machine uptime.
Cost is a central customer question and must be made clear.
Reaction time and machine uptime were identified as concrete ways in which the customer could benefit.
